title: February 28 Incident
summary: On 27-28 February 1947 a confrontation between Monopoly Bureau agents and a cigarette vendor in Taipei, followed by shooting of protesters, set off island-wide unrest against Nationalist rule. After troops landed at Keelung on 8 March, the government crushed the unrest and then arrested and executed many people. No exact death toll exists; estimates run from about 10,000 to about 30,000.

uncertainty.note: The spark was on the evening of 27 February; protests began 28 February. The end date is the start of the "Ching-hsiang" clean-up campaign; arrests and executions continued afterwards.

where.modern_name: Taipei, Taiwan (unrest spread across the island)
where.historical_name: Taipei, Taiwan Province, Republic of China

importance.justification: A massacre that shaped decades of Taiwanese politics, martial law and memory, and still a central point of reckoning for the island.

audience_note: Describes killings of civilians by troops, executions and political repression. The death toll is contested and there is no exact count.

sources.title: Taiwan's White Terror: Remembering the 228 Incident

reviewer_note: Least sure of the toll: the 228 Memorial Foundation calls 10,000-20,000 the most cited figure, FPRI quotes 18,000-28,000, and Taipei Times says around 30,000; none is a count. Pin is Taipei, where the events started; unrest and killings occurred island-wide.
author: historian-agent:o-s8

beats.caption: After a vendor was beaten and a bystander shot, crowds protested in Taipei and military police fired on them on 28 February.
Unrest spread across Taiwan; the 21st Division landed at Keelung on 8 March and began crackdowns and killings.
No exact count exists; one cited range is 18,000 to 28,000 deaths. Martial law followed and was not lifted until 1987.
